title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: Never confuse an oversold 4-hour bounce inside a Stage 4 breakdown with a Stage 2 institutional accumulation base. Wait for the major weekly averages to turn upward before risking capital.
epigraph.author: Weinstein Stage Discipline

web_blocks.html: Between November 13 and November 20, 2026, JPMorgan Chase broke decisively down from Stage 3 consolidation into Stage 4 (Declining) [34]. Shares closed November 20 at $310.68 in TradingView and options feeds ($310.53 in the daily facts ledger), down 2.98% on the session and -10.31% for the week [34]. The breakdown occurred on heavy institutional distribution: volume hit 12.52 million shares, or 1.73x the 30-day average (1.89x the 20-day average in the facts ledger) [34]. More critically, JPM sliced through its 50-day SMA ($337.35), 30-week SMA ($334.16), 200-day SMA ($325.20), Pivot S1 ($326.16), Pivot S2 ($315.27), and the prior $322.51 invalidation stop.

Stage Classification Disclosure (snapshots Stage 4 vs. facts Stage 1): Transparent auditing requires flagging a divergence between our two quantitative feeds [34]. The daily facts ledger mechanically tags JPM as Stage 1 (Basing) solely because $310.53 sits 0.17 ATR above its 63-day base low ($309.18). However, the same facts ledger confirms a FALLING/FLAT 50-day SMA ($337.35, down from $346.04 twenty-one days ago), a -3.39 ATR deficit below the 50-day SMA, and negative 63-day relative strength (-3.22% vs. S&P 500). Meanwhile, the live TradingView snapshots evaluator classifies JPM as STAGE_4 (CAP_REJECTED / AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN) because price sits -7.91% below the 50-day SMA, -7.03% below the 30-week SMA, -7.25% below the 10-week EMA ($334.97), and -4.46% below the 200-day SMA. We adopt STAGE_4 as the authoritative technical classification and reject new capital until a true base and Stage 2 reclaim form.

web_blocks.title: Why the Stage-4-Reclaim Geometry Fails the 1.50:1 Risk-Reward Gate

web_blocks.html: To avoid self-contradiction, we must measure new-entry risk-reward strictly from the price zone where JPM actually exits Stage 4. Advertising a deep knife-catch zone at $285 while instructing traders to wait for a Stage 2 reclaim above $334 would contradict our own trigger. Exiting Stage 4 requires JPM to build a Stage 1 base and reclaim its 30-week SMA ($334.16) to 50-day SMA ($337.35) overhead band on expanding volume.

Now test a real structural invalidation stop beneath that reclaim band using JPM's live 14-day ATR of $7.92. Pivot S2 sits at $315.27—which is $18.89 (2.39x ATR) below $334.16 and $22.08 (2.79x ATR) below $337.35. Against our reconciled 2.50x Base Case of $302.75 stated ($284.30 HTM-adjusted), buying a $334.16–$337.35 reclaim locks in negative expected upside (-$31.41 to -$34.60 on stated TBV, or -$49.86 to -$53.05 HTM-adjusted) against $18.89 to $22.08 of stop risk. That produces a negative reward-to-risk ratio (< 0:1), failing our mandatory 1.50:1 minimum by a wide margin. Even if you test the 200-day SMA ($325.20) to 40-week EMA ($328.20), JPM remains both below its 30-week and 50-day averages and above our $302.75 Base value.

Our options desk reaches the same disciplined conclusion [34]. Although JPM shows a classic DISLOCATION_AT_MAJOR_SHELF pattern near its $309.18 sixty-three-day low and $315.27 Pivot S2, the 4-hour RSI sits deeply oversold at 21.97 with intraday_4h_turn: false (4H EMA20 at $329.80). A $310/$330 bull call debit spread costs $9.57 for $10.43 maximum gain, a 1.09:1 payoff below the 1.25:1 minimum threshold. With the S&P 500 in a confirmed Downtrend (10 distribution days in 25 sessions and only 38.8% of stocks above their 50-DMA) and peers BAC, WFC, and C all trapped in Stage 4, standing aside preserves capital cleanly.

book_paragraphs: Great businesses regularly go through ugly technical phases, and November 20, 2026 delivered a textbook reminder. Within five trading days, JPMorgan Chase dropped 10.31% from $346.19 to $310.68, slicing cleanly through its 50-day moving average ($337.35), its 30-week moving average ($334.16), its 200-day moving average ($325.20), Pivot S2 ($315.27), and our prior $322.51 invalidation stop. Volume swelled to 12.52 million shares—roughly 1.73 times its 30-day average—proving that institutions were actively selling into the decline rather than quietly absorbing supply.

Before choosing a posture, let us reconcile an important quantitative split in our market ledgers. Our daily facts file tags JPMorgan as Stage 1 (Basing) because $310.53 sits just 0.17 ATR above its 63-day low of $309.18. Yet that very same ledger records a falling 50-day moving average, a 3.39-ATR deficit beneath it, and negative 63-day relative strength (-3.22%). Our TradingView stage evaluator rightly overrides that mechanical base tag and assigns Stage 4 (CAP_REJECTED), because price sits well beneath falling weekly and daily trend lines across all timeframes.

Checking all three timeframes—weekly, daily, and four-hour—confirms there is no turn yet. Weekly RSI sits at 39.55 below the 30-week SMA ($334.16); daily RSI sits at 30.72 below the 200-day SMA ($325.20); and 4-hour RSI sits at an oversold 21.97 beneath its 4-hour 20-EMA ($329.80) with zero upward reversal signal. Meanwhile, the broader S&P 500 is locked in a Downtrend with 10 distribution days and only 38.8% of tracked stocks above their 50-day moving averages, while peers Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup all sit in Stage 4.

Crucially, look at what happens when we combine Chapter 7's reconciled fair value with Chapter 8's reclaim chart. To exit Stage 4 without catching a falling knife, JPMorgan must reclaim its 30-week to 50-day moving-average ceiling ($334.16 to $337.35). With a daily ATR of $7.92, placing a real structural stop beneath the base at Pivot S2 ($315.27) creates $18.89 to $22.08 of risk per share. Against our reconciled 2.50x Base Case of $302.75 stated ($284.30 HTM-adjusted), buying a $334.16–$337.35 reclaim leaves negative reward-to-risk (< 0:1)—far below our 1.50-to-1 hurdle.

book_subsections.title: Why Oversold 4-Hour Readings Are Not a Buy Signal
paragraphs: New investors often look at a 4-hour RSI of 21.97 and a daily RSI of 30.72 and assume the stock must snap back tomorrow. In a bull market Stage 2 pullback, oversold readings near a rising 50-day average often mark clean entries. In a Stage 4 breakdown during an S&P 500 Downtrend, however, oversold oscillators frequently stay oversold—or bounce briefly into broken moving averages before rolling lower again.

Notice that our options desk tested whether a defined-risk $310/$330 bull call spread offered cheap convexity on this dislocation. It did not: paying $9.57 for a $20-wide spread leaves only $10.43 of maximum profit (1.09:1 reward-to-risk, below our 1.25:1 minimum), while the 4-hour chart has yet to turn up. Standing aside is the disciplined move.

Look closely at the institutional volume footprint behind that 10.31% weekly drop. On November 20 alone, 12.52 million shares changed hands—nearly double the 20-day average—closing near the intraday session lows and right beside the 63-day base low of $309.18. When heavy volume accompanies a break below both the 50-day and 200-day moving averages across an entire sector (with Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup all printing Stage 4 breakdowns simultaneously), disciplined investors let institutional sellers finish liquidating before stepping back in.

book_subsections.title: Zero Contradiction Between Reclaim Triggers and Risk-Reward Math
paragraphs: Always verify that your trigger price and your risk-reward table live in the same reality. Some analysts fall into a hedging trap: they advertise a cheap support buy zone below the market to make reward-to-risk look impressive, while writing in fine print that you should wait for a breakout above resistance before buying.

We refuse that contradiction. Because Stage 4 rules forbid catching a falling knife at $310.68, the earliest disciplined re-entry trigger sits above the 30-week and 50-day moving averages ($334.16 to $337.35). Once you anchor your stop properly at Pivot S2 ($315.27, more than 2.3x ATR below reclaim), negative upside to our $302.75 stated ($284.30 HTM-adjusted) Base Case proves that patience—and a formal REJECTED capital posture—is mathematically warranted.

Keep the full moving-average ladder taped beside your screen as JPMorgan works through this Stage 4 phase: $309.18 marks the 63-day swing low, $315.27 marks Pivot S2, $325.20 marks the 200-day moving average, $328.20 marks the 40-week EMA, $334.16 marks the 30-week SMA, and $337.35 marks the falling 50-day SMA. Until price climbs back above the upper shelf ($334.16–$337.35) with rising volume and a flattening 50-day slope, the trend remains broken.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: JPMorgan Chase broke below its 50D, 30W, and 200D moving averages on 1.73x distribution volume into Stage 4 ($310.68). Reclaiming the $334.16–$337.35 trend band above a $315.27 structural stop yields negative upside (< 0:1) to our reconciled $302.75 stated ($284.30 HTM-adjusted) Base Case.
